vignette: Ahmed, a 38-year-old Middle Eastern man, has been working as a hairdresser in the heart of downtown for over a decade. His hands are deft and his eyes sharp, spotting trends and styling preferences with an uncanny precision that has earned him a loyal clientele. However, beneath this professional veneer lies a narrative shaped by a life-threatening illness he endured two years ago. Ahmed was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) when he was 36. The diagnosis came as a shock; the night before his bone marrow biopsy, he had been styling hair and laughing with friends at a local café. The next morning, he found himself in a hospital bed, surrounded by medical professionals explaining the severity of his condition. He describes that moment as the most disorienting of his life. "It was like being told I had to live underwater when all my life, I breathed air," Ahmed says. Throughout his chemotherapy treatment, Ahmed experienced bouts of severe nausea and fatigue. Each day felt like a battle against the unseen enemy within him-his own body attacking itself. He recalls one particularly challenging cycle of chemo where he was bedridden for over a week, unable to leave his hospital room. The sterile smell of antiseptic and the constant hum of medical equipment became part of his daily reality. The trauma of this experience has left lasting imprints on Ahmed's life. Even now, two years after his treatment ended, the shadow of that time lingers in unexpected ways. For instance, he often feels an overwhelming sense of dread when passing by hospitals or even seeing hospital signs while driving. "Every time I see a white coat or hear someone cough, my heart races like it's about to jump out of my chest," Ahmed explains. At work, the environment is starkly different from the sterile confines of his treatment rooms, but he still encounters triggers. The sharp smell of hair dye and chemicals can sometimes evoke memories of chemotherapy treatments, making him feel lightheaded or nauseous. He has noticed that these sensations are strongest when he's dealing with a particularly difficult cut or style-when all eyes are on him and the pressure feels immense. Ahmed also experiences intrusive thoughts and flashbacks intermittently. Often, while styling hair for clients, he finds himself suddenly transported back to those hospital moments. His mind replays conversations with doctors, scans of medical reports, and even the sound of beeping machines. These episodes can leave him feeling detached from his surroundings, a phenomenon he describes as "floating above my own body." Moreover, Ahmed has noticed an increased startle response. Even small noises-like clippers suddenly turning on or a doorbell ringing unexpectedly-can cause him to jump violently and feel momentarily disoriented. Despite these challenges, Ahmed continues to work diligently at his salon. His clients often comment on how calm and collected he appears. However, beneath the surface, this façade is maintained through constant mental and emotional effort. He frequently checks in with himself throughout the day, taking deep breaths and grounding exercises like touching different textures or focusing on a specific scent that reminds him of home. Ahmed's life continues to be marked by both his past trauma and his ongoing efforts to reclaim normalcy. His work as a hairdresser serves not only as an occupation but also as a source of stability and comfort in the midst of his ongoing struggle with PTSD symptoms.
